evidence.experimental_conditions: RIPT on 91 individuals (84 female, 7 male), deodorant body spray containing 98.2% SD Alcohol 40-B, 0.1 ml per patch, patches applied for 24 h every Monday, Wednesday, Friday for 3 consecutive weeks, challenge in week 6, reactions scored 24 and 48 h after removal.
evidence.support_text: CTFA (1984a) reported results of an RIPT conducted on 91 individuals (84 female and 7 male) to determine if a deodorant body spray containing 98.2% SD Alcohol 40-B induces skin irritation and/or allergic sensitization. Ten patches were placed on the upper backs of the subjects (five on each side). About 0.1 ml of the test material was added to the patches before applications. The patches were applied every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday for 3 consecutive weeks, for 24 h. A challenge was conducted in week 6 of the study, and the reactions were scored 24 and 48 h after removal. Only four reactions occurred throughout the entire study, including the challenge phase, in which those subjects received a mark of 'barely perceptible; minimal faint (light pink) uniform or spotty erythema.' It was concluded that the deodorant body spray containing 98.2% Alcohol 40-B does not exhibit any potential for inducing allergic sensitization.

evidence.experimental_conditions: semiocclusive patch, 0.2 ml, 24h, 3 times/week for 10 applications, 2-week rest, challenge on original and new site, scored at 24 and 48h
evidence.support_text: A cream containing 5% Tocopherol was tested in a repeat-insult patch test (RIPT) on 113 subjects. The test material was applied semiocclusively for 24 hours, three times per week for 10 applications, followed by a 2-week rest and a challenge. The cream was found not to be a sensitizer.

The test was performed on human participants.

evidence.support_text: An RIPT of a lotion containing 0.1% Tocopheryl Acetate was completed using 110 subjects (18 males, 92 females) with semiocclusive patching. No reactions were observed during induction or challenge. The lotion was not a primary irritant or sensitizer.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Induction: 100 ppm MIT, 0.15 mL, occlusive Webril patch, 23 hours, 4 times/week for 3 weeks. Challenge: 100 ppm MIT, 0.15 mL, 24 hours. Evaluation 48, 72, 96 hours post-challenge. 98 subjects.
evidence.support_text: In an RIPT involving 98 subjects who had patch tested negative for 100 ppm Kathon CG, 100 ppm MIT was applied during induction (0.15 mL, occlusive Webril patches, 23 hours, 4 times/week for 3 weeks) and then challenged with 100 ppm MIT (0.15 mL, 24 hours). One subject had a grade 4 reaction on the fifth day of induction and was determined sensitized. No other subjects reacted, and the authors concluded that 100 ppm MIT does not induce skin sensitization in human subjects.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Induction: 200, 300, 400, 500, 600 ppm MIT (50% formulation), 0.2 mL, occlusive Webril patches, 24 hours, 3 times/week for 3 weeks. Rest periods: 1 week (200, 300 ppm) or 10–15 days (400–600 ppm). Challenge: same concentration as induction, 24 hours. Evaluation 48 and 72 hours post-challenge. Subjects: 100 (200 ppm), 98 (300 ppm), 116 (400 ppm), 210 (500 ppm), 214 (600 ppm).
evidence.support_text: In a series of RIPTs evaluating 50% MIT at 200, 300, 400, 500, and 600 ppm (0.2 mL, occlusive patches, 24 hours, 3 times/week for 3 weeks), no signs of skin irritation were observed during induction. Only 1 subject in the 400-ppm group and 1 in the 500-ppm group had an incidence of erythema response. It was concluded that MIT up to 600 ppm is not a dermal sensitizer.

Sensitization was evaluated at three to four weeks by applying 0.1 cc of 0.1% DNCB to the opposite forearm; positive reactions were defined by induration and/or vesiculation.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 1% cinnamaldehyde in petrolatum, applied to upper back with Finn Chambers and Scanpor for 48-72 h, reactions read at removal and 48-120 h after removal, scoring per NACDG modification of ICDRG
evidence.support_text: In a worldwide multicenter study to investigate fragrance sensitization in patients with suspected fragrance allergies, 167 patients were patch tested with fragrance materials. Test materials were applied to the upper back with Finn Chambers® and Scanpor® for a period of 48–72 h. Reactions were read at patch removal and then re-examined in most cases usually between 48 and 120 h after patch removal. Reactions were scored according to the North American Contact Dermatitis Group's modification of the ICDRG scoring criteria. Reactions to 1% cinnamaldehyde in petrolatum were observed in 14.4% of the patients (Larsen et al., 1996).
